A single score prices one move class (advancing) and cannot reproduce how work was actually chosen; taking several selection patterns at once seems to give up the clarity of one winner.

Unbounded exploration absorbs effort and is deferred again and again instead of being decided; a stop rule set afterwards is moved to fit the result.
Long all-out runs look productive and some real work has no visible end for a long time; an end-to-end demonstration chosen too early fails and has to be cut back.
Building at once feels faster, and a discovery packet that also implements gives no checkpoint between the finding and the code.

The halfway house can quietly become the destination and close the target by default; or the target is built first and commits shapes before anyone knows which matter.
Held items without a re-arm condition are either forgotten or re-asked in every report.
Held items whose condition has quietly been met wait for someone to notice.
A bare list hands the whole judgment back; a single recommendation hides the alternatives; and an unrecorded pick teaches nothing.
A work list says what is wanted, not what can be done next; the most wanted item is often blocked.
Dependency claims are also often broader than the real dependency: one criterion depends, the rest could run now.
Groundwork frees nothing at once, so ordering by immediate unblocking ranks it low; and a day of groundwork reported as output overstates it.

Giraffe pilot 2 measured the split: two items had cones of 14 but unblocked nothing alone.
Throughput pulls toward the next new item, and building on the defect looks like progress until the result has to be retracted.
The opposite mistake also happens: stopping the line is read as "pause everything until the repair queue is drained", which stops selection altogether.
Audit, held, close, absent, and empty-way placements are not work placements.
The protocol or the plan names an author (bell coding to Codex), and following it blindly means dispatches that die mid-job.
Unused allowance is lost at a reset, but spending it too aggressively starves interactive work.
Cheap work can crowd out the item others wait on, and a run of cheap wins can look like progress while the hard part waits.
Splitting a hard problem into cheap pieces can also hide that its parts depend on each other.
Cheap pieces close sooner and look better on a count, and splitting invites declaring the whole done when one piece lands.
The opposite error is choosing the hard thing because it is hard.
Deadline work displaces work with more leverage, and scope pressure invites claims that will not hold.
Doing every ask at once bypasses readiness and repair; paraphrasing the ask loses what was wanted; and an ask can turn out to be impossible.
Plans are often written in another order (the order pieces were thought of), and the item many others need may be harder or less visible than a cheap uncoupled one.
Committed money with unspecified deliverables sits idle; chasing leads mechanically turns into a PR farm; internal scores do not see revenue at all.
Doing it now breaks scope; not doing it lets it evaporate; writing a whole mission for it is too much.
